final_proof:
The claim as stated is false. Let \(T_1\) be the one-point space \(\{p\}\), let \(T_2=\mathbb{Q}\) with the topology inherited from \(\mathbb{R}\), and define \(f(p)=0\). The space \(T_1\) is compact and locally connected, \(T_2\) is Hausdorff, and \(f\) is continuous. However, \(\mathbb{Q}\) is not locally connected.

Indeed, every connected subset of \(\mathbb{Q}\) has at most one point. If \(A\subseteq\mathbb{Q}\) contains distinct points \(a<b\), choose an irrational number \(r\) with \(a<r<b\). Then
\[
A\cap(-\infty,r)\quad\text{and}\quad A\cap(r,\infty)
\]
are disjoint, nonempty subsets which are both open and closed in \(A\), and their union is \(A\). Hence \(A\) is disconnected. Thus the only connected subsets of \(\mathbb{Q}\) are singletons. No singleton is a neighborhood of its point in \(\mathbb{Q}\), since \(\mathbb{Q}\) has no isolated points. Therefore \(\mathbb{Q}\) is not locally connected. This counterexample satisfies all the stated hypotheses and disproves the conclusion.

The natural corrected theorem is that \(f(T_1)\), endowed with the subspace topology inherited from \(T_2\), is locally connected. In particular, the original conclusion becomes true if one adds the hypothesis that \(f\) is surjective.

To prove the corrected theorem, write \(X=S_1\), let \(Z=f(X)\), and regard \(f\) as a continuous surjection \(g:X\to Z\). Since \(T_2\) is Hausdorff, its subspace \(Z\) is Hausdorff. Fix \(z\in Z\) and an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\) in \(Z\). The fiber
\[
F=g^{-1}(\{z\})
\]
is closed in \(X\), because singletons are closed in a Hausdorff space, and is therefore compact. Moreover, \(g^{-1}(U)\) is an open set containing \(F\).

For every \(x\in F\), local connectedness of \(X\) supplies a connected open set \(V_x\) such that
\[
x\in V_x\subseteq g^{-1}(U).
\]
By compactness of \(F\), finitely many of these sets, say \(V_1,\ldots,V_n\), cover \(F\). Put
\[
W=V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_n.
\]
Each \(g(V_i)\) is connected by continuity and contains \(z\), because \(V_i\) was chosen around a point of \(F\). Consequently,
\[
C=g(W)=g(V_1)\cup\cdots\cup g(V_n)
\]
is connected. Moreover, \(C\subseteq U\).

We next show that \(C\) is a neighborhood of \(z\), although it need not itself be open. The set \(X\setminus W\) is compact, so \(g(X\setminus W)\) is compact and hence closed in the Hausdorff space \(Z\). Because \(F\subseteq W\), we have \(z\notin g(X\setminus W)\). Thus
\[
N=Z\setminus g(X\setminus W)
\]
is an open neighborhood of \(z\). Furthermore, \(N\subseteq g(W)=C\): if \(y\in N\), surjectivity gives some \(x\in X\) with \(g(x)=y\), and such an \(x\) cannot belong to \(X\setminus W\), so \(x\in W\). Hence
\[
z\in N\subseteq C\subseteq U.
\]
Thus every open neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\) contains a connected neighborhood \(C\) of \(z\).

For completeness, this implies local connectedness in the usual open-basis sense. Let \(K\) be the connected component of \(U\) containing \(z\). Since \(C\) is connected, contains \(z\), and lies in \(U\), we have \(C\subseteq K\). Because \(C\) contains the open neighborhood \(N\) of \(z\), the point \(z\) is an interior point of \(K\). Applying the same argument at every point of every component of \(U\) shows that every component of \(U\) is open. Hence \(K\) is a connected open neighborhood of \(z\) contained in \(U\). Since \(z\) and \(U\) were arbitrary, \(Z=f(X)\) is locally connected. If \(f\) is surjective, then \(Z=T_2\), proving the corrected version of the original assertion.
